stem: For compatible transformation matrices A,B,C, which change is always allowed without changing ABC?

options.text: Replace AB with A+B
Replace(AB)C with A(BC)
Replace ABC with BAC
Replace ABC with CBA

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 6: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: A skew-symmetric matrix satisfies S=-S^T and has zero diagonal. For Omega=(Omega_x,Omega_y,Omega_z)^T, S=[[0,-Omega_z,Omega_y],[Omega_z,0,-Omega_x],[-Omega_y,Omega_x,0]], and Omega×P=SP. AB is defined when columns(A)=rows(B). Multiplication is associative but not commutative in general. Transformation matrices compound to obtain end-effector position/orientation from the base.

solution.justification: The base-to-tip chain can be grouped for computation, but its order carries physical meaning.

optionExplanations.o1: Associativity permits changing parentheses while retaining order.
optionExplanations.o2: Interchanging A and B requires a special commutation property not assumed here.
optionExplanations.o3: Reversal changes the transformation chain in general.
optionExplanations.o4: Addition is not composition by matrix multiplication.

solution.simpleExplanation: The base-to-tip chain can be grouped for computation, but its order carries physical meaning.
misconceptions: Interpreting noncommutative as forbidding associativity; some special matrix pairs do commute.
examTraps: Interpreting noncommutative as forbidding associativity; some special matrix pairs do commute.

stem: Which situation matches the lecture definition of a robot kinematic singularity?

options.text: Every matrix describing the robot becomes symmetric
The robot changes its coordinate labels
A nonzero vector changes length
The Jacobian loses rank

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 7: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: The determinant is a scalar calculated from a square matrix; it indicates invertibility and acts as a scaling factor for linear transformations. Rank is the maximum number of linearly independent rows or columns. A^-1 exists if det(A)≠0 and AA^-1=I; A^-1=adj(A)/det(A). Loss of Jacobian rank is a singularity; the slide writes det(J)=0.

solution.justification: Singularity concerns lost independent directions, not merely large or small numerical entries.

optionExplanations.o1: This removes an independent velocity-mapping direction; the slide connects it to failure of inversion.
optionExplanations.o2: Symmetry is unrelated to the rank-loss definition.
optionExplanations.o3: Renaming coordinates alone is not a rank loss.
optionExplanations.o4: Scaling alone need not make a mapping singular.

solution.simpleExplanation: Singularity concerns lost independent directions, not merely large or small numerical entries.

stem: Why does the definition explicitly exclude x=0 from being an eigenvector?

options.text: A0 is undefined
Zero vectors have infinite norm
All eigenvalues must be nonzero
A0=lambda 0 holds for every lambda and cannot identify an eigen-direction

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 8: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: For square A, an eigenvector x is nonzero and satisfies Ax=lambda x. The characteristic equation is det(lambda I-A)=0. Eigenvectors/eigenvalues represent principal directions and scaling factors. The slide states asymptotic stability when real parts of all system-matrix eigenvalues are negative.

solution.justification: The equation is informative only when the vector supplies a genuine direction.

optionExplanations.o1: The zero vector supplies no direction and would make the equation vacuous.
optionExplanations.o2: Any finite matrix can multiply the compatible zero vector.
optionExplanations.o4: A singular square matrix can have a zero eigenvalue with a nonzero eigenvector.

solution.simpleExplanation: The equation is informative only when the vector supplies a genuine direction.

stem: For the displayed Bayes formula, which condition is necessary to divide by P(B)?

options.text: P(A)=P(B)
A and B must be independent

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 12: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: Conditional probability updates event A given B. Bayes formula: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Prior means before evidence; posterior means after new evidence. Localization estimates P(x|z) for state x and measurement z. Speech decoding uses P(i|o)=P(o|i)P(i)/P(o).

solution.justification: The denominator must be nonzero; independence is not a prerequisite.

optionExplanations.o1: Conditioning by this elementary formula requires positive evidence probability.
optionExplanations.o2: That would produce division by zero.
optionExplanations.o3: Equal event probabilities are not required.
optionExplanations.o4: Bayes rule is useful precisely when they may be dependent.

solution.simpleExplanation: The denominator must be nonzero; independence is not a prerequisite.

stem: A robot updates its state estimate after observing noisy sensor data z. Which quantity is its posterior state belief?

options.text: P(z)

P(z|x)
P(x)

citations.evidenceText: Conditional probability updates event A given B. Bayes formula: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Prior means before evidence; posterior means after new evidence. Localization estimates P(x|z) for state x and measurement z. Speech decoding uses P(i|o)=P(o|i)P(i)/P(o).

solution.justification: State given observation is the posterior; observation given state is the likelihood.

stem: Which expression is the mean of a continuous variable with density f_X?
subtopic: PMF versus PDF and continuous expectation
tags: PMF versus PDF and continuous expectation

options.text: Integral over realx of x f_X(x) dx
Integral over realx of f_X(x) dx
The largest value of f_X(x)
Sum of all valuesx without probability weighting

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 13: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: A random variable is a function X:Omega→R mapping experimental outcomes to real numbers. Discrete mean E(X)=sum_i x_i P(X=x_i); continuous mean E(X)=integral from -infinity to infinity of x f_X(x) dx. Discrete variables use PMFs; continuous variables use PDFs. Expected robot reward is a probability-weighted average.

solution.justification: The factorx changes normalization into an average value.

optionExplanations.o1: The slide weights each continuous value by its density and integrates.
optionExplanations.o2: For a normalized PDF this is 1, not the mean.
optionExplanations.o3: A peak density is not a mean.
optionExplanations.o4: This ignores the probability law and is not the displayed expectation.

solution.simpleExplanation: The factorx changes normalization into an average value.

stem: If all candidate models have the same positive prior probability and the likelihood has a unique maximizer, how do MLE and MAP compare?
assumptions: Finite candidate set, equal positive priors, fixed data with positive evidence, and unique likelihood maximum.

options.text: MLE becomes undefined
MAP ignores the likelihood completely
They select the same model
MAP must select a different model

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 15: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: MLE finds parameter values that best explain observed data only. MAP incorporates prior knowledge. Posterior P(mu_m|s), likelihood P(s|mu_m), prior P(mu_m), and evidence P(s) are distinguished. The displayed formula writes MAP=arg max P(mu_m|s)=P(s|mu_m)P(mu_m)/P(s), conflating an argmax with a probability.

solution.justification: A uniform prior adds no preference among the candidates.

optionExplanations.o1: Multiplying every likelihood by the same positive constant leaves its ordering unchanged.
optionExplanations.o2: A prior affects ordering only when its relative values differ.
optionExplanations.o4: The posterior still includes the likelihood factor.

solution.simpleExplanation: A uniform prior adds no preference among the candidates.

stem: Which wall-distance estimator uses the extra information associated with MAP in the lecture example?

options.text: One assuming extra data guarantees zero error
One combining new range data with prior map knowledge
One using sensor data but no prior model information
One ignoring both sensor readings and the map

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 16: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: Bayesian updating begins with a prior; a new observation updates the belief; the posterior becomes the next prior. Wall-distance example: MLE uses measurements, MAP combines measurements with prior map knowledge. The slide says further sensor data makes estimates more accurate/stable, without specifying noise/model assumptions.

solution.justification: Prior knowledge contributes another source of information; it does not magically remove all noise.

optionExplanations.o1: That combination is the stated contrast with data-only estimation.
optionExplanations.o2: This reflects the example’s MLE side.
optionExplanations.o3: That is not estimation from either source.
optionExplanations.o4: The example offers no such exact finite-data guarantee.

solution.simpleExplanation: Prior knowledge contributes another source of information; it does not magically remove all noise.
misconceptions: Treating the slide’s qualitative accuracy statement as an unconditional guarantee under biased sensors or a wrong model.
examTraps: Treating the slide’s qualitative accuracy statement as an unconditional guarantee under biased sensors or a wrong model.

stem: Given q_ddot+3q_dot+2q=u, choose x1=q and x2=q_dot. Which first-order pair is equivalent?
assumptions: The second-order equation and state definitions are stipulated in the question.

options.text: x1_dot=x2; x2_dot=2x1+3x2+u
x1_dot=u; x2_dot=x1
x1_dot=x2; x2_dot=−2x1−3x2+u
x1_dot=x1; x2_dot=−2x1−3x2+u

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 18: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: Continuous-time LTI state-space models use first-order differential equations. State equation x_dot(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t), output equation y(t)=Cx(t). A higher-order equation can be broken into a vector of first-order equations. A robot-arm state can include position and velocity.

solution.justification: Introducing a velocity state lowers equation order without removing the dynamics.

optionExplanations.o1: The first equation defines velocity; the second rearranges the given dynamics.
optionExplanations.o2: The first derivative ofq isq_dot=x2, notq=x1.
optionExplanations.o3: Moving restoring and damping terms to the right gives negative signs.
optionExplanations.o4: This discards the given second-order relationship.

solution.simpleExplanation: Introducing a velocity state lowers equation order without removing the dynamics.

stem: Which statement describes resolution completeness as presented?

options.text: Its success probability must equal 1 after exactly one random sample
It always finds the least-cost route regardless of representation
The planner can find a solution when the discretization is fine enough
It finds every continuous-space solution on every coarse grid

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 27: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: Completeness concerns finding a solution if one exists. The slide distinguishes complete, resolution complete (fine enough discretization), and probabilistically complete (success probability tends to 1 as time tends to infinity). It says genetic algorithms may find near-optimal paths but do not guarantee the absolute shortest path in finitely many steps. Unqualified claims about A* and genetic algorithms require assumptions.

solution.justification: A discretized map must be fine enough to represent the relevant route.

optionExplanations.o1: This is the slide’s grid-resolution qualification.
optionExplanations.o2: A coarse grid may fail to represent a narrow feasible passage.
optionExplanations.o3: This is neither the resolution criterion nor the probabilistic limit criterion.
optionExplanations.o4: Resolution completeness alone is not an optimality guarantee.

solution.simpleExplanation: A discretized map must be fine enough to represent the relevant route.

options.text: The probability of success decreases to 0 with more time

No; opposite off-diagonal entries are also required
